gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on the same WRMS scale the new TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII are rated at 0.25% wow and flutter. That is 11–13 times the 0.019% to 0.022% the Nakamichi Dragon and Sony TC-KA7ES are rated at. The new decks' frequency response is also quoted at a looser ±4 dB and stops at 15 kHz, while the vintage decks reach 22 kHz at ±3 dB.
standout_why: StereoNET (cited in all three chats) gives no wow-and-flutter figure for any deck. It lists only the TEAC W-1200 at about $549 with 'noise reduction' and 'parallel dubbing', and only head count and Dolby type for the Nakamichi and Revox models. ChatGPT's own answers say 'Not as high-fidelity as a restored vintage flagship' with no number behind it. I couldn't open Portcycling (cited in one chat): it returned HTTP 403. Our current page has no fidelity column at all. Specs are scattered across maker sheets and Wikipedia, but none of the results puts them side by side on one standard.
decides: It confirms the split pick and puts a number on it. For playback fidelity, a serviced vintage 3-head deck is in a different class: rated speed stability is 11–13 times better on the same WRMS basis. On paper, though, S/N is not the gap: the TEAC's 59 dB A-weighted and the TC-KA7ES's 57 dB with Dolby off are about the same. For the 'buy new' pick, the TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII have identical makers' deck specs (0.25% WRMS; 30 Hz–15 kHz ±4 dB on Type II tape; Dolby B-equivalent playback NR only). So the choice between them comes down to price, the remote, and rack mounting, not sound. Footnote for the table: the Revox B215's '0.1%' is a DIN 45507 peak-weighted maximum, not WRMS, so it can't be ranked against the 0.25% WRMS figures. Reviewers measured it at 0.01–0.042% RMS.

findings.label: Wow and flutter (maker spec)
findings.note: Wikipedia quotes the Nakamichi Dragon Service Manual (1982), section 11. Craig Stark (Stereo Review, 1983 p.39; 1988 p.56) and Len Feldman (1983 p.52) confirmed it. 0.25 / 0.019 = 13.2x the TEAC/Tascam rating on the same WRMS basis.

findings.label: Frequency response (reviewer measured)
findings.value: 11–12 Hz low end and 22–24 kHz top end (depending on tape), within ±3 dB at -20 dB
findings.note: Howard Roberson (Audio, 1983–84, p.70). Stark (1983) measured a +4 dB playback treble rise at 18 kHz. Stark (1988) measured dynamic range at 54 / 56.5 / 59 dB for Type I / II / IV.

findings.label: Wow and flutter
findings.note: Reproduction of Sony's 1995 catalogue specs (¥120,000 at launch). 0.25 / 0.022 = 11.4x the TEAC/Tascam rating.

findings.label: Frequency response and S/N
findings.value: 15 Hz–22 kHz ±3 dB (EIAJ, -20 dB, metal); 15 Hz–16 kHz ±3 dB (-4 dB, metal); S/N 57 dB Dolby off, metal (EIAJ); 80 dB with Dolby S
findings.note: 3-head (erase, record, play). Its Dolby-off S/N of 57 dB is close to the TEAC's 59 dB A-weighted (NR state not stated), so S/N does not separate new from vintage on paper. The 80 dB figure needs Dolby S encode and decode.

findings.label: Wow and flutter (maker spec vs measured)
findings.value: 0.1% max per DIN 45507 / IEC 386 (Studer spec); 0.01–0.042% RMS measured
findings.note: Studer's 0.1% is a peak-weighted maximum (Willi Studer AG 1985, §7.4), not WRMS, so it can't be compared directly with 0.25% WRMS. RMS range from Roberson (Audio 1985), Stark (1986, 1988) and Feldman (1986); Feldman called the worst value of 0.042% 'remarkably low'.

findings.label: Frequency response
findings.value: 30 Hz–20 kHz +2/-3 dB (Types II and IV), 30 Hz–18 kHz (Type I), Studer spec; 9 Hz–23.1/24.5 kHz ±3 dB at -20 dB measured
findings.note: Measured figures from Howard Roberson (Audio, 1985, p.50) using Maxell UD-XLI, TDK HX-S and TDK MA-R tapes.
